create-task /create-task task47 Goal is to become comfortable in using OpenCode, Entire.io and GitHub, in combination. here are the details Create a complete, student-ready programming assignment for an **AI-Assisted Software Development** exercise. The assignment should require students to build the **same CLI application twice**: 1. **C language** 2. **Python language** The application is a **Mini HTML Parser that converts HTML content into an in-memory DOM tree**. The students must use: - **OpenCode** (`opencode.ai`) as their AI coding agent - **Entire** (`entire.io`) to capture and preserve development context, decisions, and reasoning - **Git/GitHub** for version control The purpose is not merely to build an HTML parser. The assignment should teach students how software development changes when an AI coding agent is part of the development process. --- # 1. Assignment Title Create an appropriate title such as: **Build a Mini HTML Parser — From HTML to DOM** Include a subtitle indicating that this is an **AI-Assisted Software Development** assignment. --- # 2. Learning Objectives The assignment should help students learn: - How an HTML parser works at a basic level - How a DOM is represented as a tree - Tree data structures - Recursion - Strings and parsing - File handling - Command-line arguments - Error handling - Dynamic memory and pointers in C - Classes and data structures in Python - Software modularity - Testing - Debugging - Git-based development - AI-assisted programming with OpenCode - Preserving engineering context using Entire - The difference between generating code and engineering software --- # 3. Problem Statement Given an HTML file such as: ```html

Hello

Welcome to AI Karyashala

``` the application must: 1. Read the HTML file. 2. Parse the HTML. 3. Construct an in-memory DOM tree. 4. Traverse the DOM tree. 5. Display the DOM tree in a format similar to the Linux `tree` command. The output should look like: ```text . └── html └── body ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" └── p └── "Welcome to AI Karyashala" ``` The important requirement is that the tree output must be generated by **traversing the in-memory DOM**, not by simply formatting the original HTML. --- # 4. Scope of HTML Do NOT require students to implement the complete HTML5 specification. Define a small, clear subset of HTML. The parser should initially support: - Opening tags - Closing tags - Text nodes - Nested elements - Sibling elements - Attributes - Whitespace between elements For example: ```html

Hello

Welcome

``` The parser should create a tree containing: ```text div ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" └── p [class="intro"] └── "Welcome" ``` Clearly state which HTML features are **out of scope**, such as: - JavaScript - CSS parsing - HTML entities - Browser rendering - Complete HTML5 error recovery - Comments, unless introduced as an optional extension - DOCTYPE processing, unless introduced as an optional extension - Script/style parsing --- # 5. DOM Data Model Require students to design an internal representation for the DOM. At minimum, the DOM should represent: ### Element Node - Tag name - Attributes - Children ### Text Node - Text content Explain that the exact implementation is left to the student. For example, in C they may use structures, pointers, linked lists, or dynamic arrays. In Python they may use classes, lists, dictionaries, or other suitable structures. Do not prescribe the implementation unnecessarily. --- # 6. Tree Output Requirement This is an important part of the assignment. The DOM must be displayed like the Unix `tree` command. Use: ```text ├── └── │ ``` appropriately. Example: ```text . └── html └── body ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" └── p └── "Welcome to AI Karyashala" ``` For attributes: ```text . └── html └── body ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" └── p [class="intro", id="first"] └── "Welcome to AI Karyashala" ``` Text nodes must be displayed inside quotation marks. The tree printer must be implemented by recursively traversing the DOM data structure. --- # 7. CLI Interface Define a simple command-line interface. For example: ```text domparser page.html ``` should display the DOM tree. Also introduce useful options: ```text domparser page.html --tree domparser page.html --text domparser page.html --tags p domparser page.html --find-id first domparser page.html --find-class intro ``` The exact command name can be chosen by the students, but the behavior must be documented. --- # 8. Development Phases Structure the assignment into incremental milestones. ## Phase 1 — Read HTML - Read an HTML file. - Display its contents. - Understand the input. ## Phase 2 — Tokenization / Parsing - Identify opening tags. - Identify closing tags. - Identify text. ## Phase 3 — Build DOM - Create the DOM node representation. - Build parent-child relationships. - Support nested elements. ## Phase 4 — Tree Display Traverse the DOM recursively and produce the `tree`-style output. ## Phase 5 — Attributes Support attributes such as: ```html

Hello

``` ## Phase 6 — Validation Detect basic malformed HTML. Examples: ```text Unclosed tag:

Unexpected closing tag: ``` ## Phase 7 — Queries Add simple DOM queries: ```text --find-tag p --find-id first --find-class intro ``` ## Phase 8 — Testing and Refactoring Create tests for: - Simple elements - Nested elements - Multiple siblings - Text nodes - Attributes - Empty elements - Malformed HTML - Deeply nested HTML --- # 9. C Implementation The C version should give students practice with: - `struct` - Pointers - Dynamic memory allocation - Strings - Arrays or linked lists - Tree structures - Recursion - File I/O - Command-line arguments - Error handling Do not provide the implementation. The students must design and implement the data structures themselves. --- # 10. Python Implementation The Python version should give students practice with: - Classes - Objects - Lists - Dictionaries - Strings - File handling - Exceptions - Recursion - Command-line arguments - Modular programming Again, do not provide the implementation. --- # 11. OpenCode Requirement OpenCode must be an explicit part of the assignment. Students must NOT simply ask: > "Build the complete HTML parser for me." Instead, require them to use an iterative engineering workflow. For example: ```text Problem ↓ Understand ↓ Plan ↓ Design ↓ Implement ↓ Run ↓ Test ↓ Debug ↓ Refactor ↓ Commit ``` Students should use OpenCode to: - Understand requirements - Discuss design alternatives - Create an implementation plan - Implement individual features - Generate tests - Diagnose errors - Refactor code - Review their implementation Require them to keep a record of important prompts and AI decisions. --- # 12. Entire Requirement Students must use Entire during development. The assignment should explain that the purpose is to preserve development context beyond the final source code. Students should examine what Entire records about: - Development sessions - Intent - Decisions - Changes - AI-assisted development - Reasoning/context around changes Students should be asked to compare: **Git alone** versus **Git + development context captured by Entire** The assignment should not prescribe exactly what Entire must capture; students should discover this through actual use. --- # 13. Git Requirements Each implementation must use Git. Require at least **5 meaningful commits**. Do not accept meaningless commits such as: ```text update changes final done ``` Examples of meaningful commits: ```text Create DOM node representation Implement basic HTML parser Add recursive tree printer Add attribute parsing Add malformed HTML detection Add DOM query support ``` Students should be able to explain what changed in each important commit. --- # 14. Two Implementations Students must create: ```text dom-parser-c/ dom-parser-python/ ``` Both implementations must support the same input and produce equivalent DOM tree output. The goal is NOT to copy the C implementation into Python. Students should make appropriate language-specific design decisions. --- # 15. Sample Input Files Create several sample HTML files for the assignment. ### simple.html ```html

Hello

``` ### nested.html ```html

Title

Hello

``` ### attributes.html ```html

Hello

World

``` ### siblings.html ```html
  • One
  • Two
  • Three
``` ### malformed.html Provide examples containing: - Missing closing tags - Unexpected closing tags - Incorrect nesting --- # 16. Expected Output For each sample input, provide expected tree-style output. Make the examples sufficiently clear that students can test their programs against them. --- # 17. Testing Require students to create automated tests where appropriate. Tests should cover: - Parsing - DOM construction - Tree traversal - Attributes - Text nodes - Error detection - Queries Also require students to perform manual CLI testing. --- # 18. Final Comparison Students must compare the two implementations. Require them to answer questions such as: 1. Which implementation was easier to develop? 2. Why? 3. How did memory management affect the C implementation? 4. What did Python make easier? 5. What was difficult for the AI agent? 6. Where did the AI generate incorrect or poor code? 7. How did they verify AI-generated code? 8. What design decisions did they make themselves? 9. How did OpenCode change their development workflow? 10. What did Entire preserve that Git alone did not? 11. What would another developer need to understand the project six months later? 12. Is source code alone a complete record of software development when AI agents are involved? --- # 19. Final Deliverables Each student must submit: ```text project/ ├── c/ ├── python/ ├── tests/ ├── samples/ ├── README.md └── development-notes/ ``` The exact structure may be adjusted by the student. The repository must contain: - C implementation - Python implementation - Sample HTML files - Tests - README - Git history - OpenCode development evidence - Entire development context - Final comparison/reflection --- # 20. Evaluation Rubric Create a clear rubric totaling 100 marks. Include categories such as: - DOM design — 15 - HTML parsing — 15 - Tree construction — 15 - Tree-style output — 10 - Attributes and queries — 10 - Error handling — 10 - Testing — 10 - C implementation quality — 5 - Python implementation quality — 5 - OpenCode usage — 3 - Entire usage — 2 Adjust the distribution if necessary, but make **actual engineering quality** more important than simply completing features. --- # 21. Important Rules Include these rules prominently: 1. Do not use an existing HTML/DOM parser library. 2. Do not copy an implementation from the Internet. 3. AI-generated code must be understood and verified. 4. Students must be able to explain their own implementation. 5. OpenCode is a development assistant, not a substitute for understanding. 6. Git commits must reflect actual development. 7. Entire must be used throughout development, not added at the end. 8. C and Python implementations must be independently developed. --- # 22. Final Reflection End the assignment with a reflection section titled: **What Does Software Engineering Look Like When AI Writes Code?** Ask students to write a short reflection addressing: > If an AI coding agent can generate a large portion of the source code, what becomes more important for a software engineer? Include prompts around: - Problem understanding - System design - Decomposition - Asking good questions - Verification - Testing - Debugging - Reviewing AI output - Making engineering decisions - Preserving development context --- ## Output expected from you Create the complete assignment as a polished, student-ready document. Do not implement the parser. Do not provide the solution. Do not provide C or Python source code. The final document should contain enough information for a student to start the assignment independently while still leaving the important design and implementation decisions to the student.

Pick the task number and base name - Next number = highest existing `docs/taskN/` + 1. - `` is snake_case and shared by all files (e.g. `bitwise_operators`, `address_variables`). Worksheet file is `_worksheet.md`. ### 3. Propose an outline — THIS IS THE REVIEW GATE Do **not** create any files yet. Present a written outline and ask the user to review and discuss it. Include: - **Task number, title, and base filename.** - **Worksheet**: the "golden rule" blockquote idea; the ordered list of iterations, each as a one-line idea plus what the student *sets up* and *observes*; any C programs to be written; the practice set; the reference-table topics; and a note that a Telugu "New Words" table will close it. Note that questions reveal no answers and that **titles must not give away what to observe**. - **Answers**: mirrors the question numbering, every answer with reasoning, closing "pattern to notice" note. - **What will be verified** (programs compiled, arithmetic/traces checked). Then explicitly invite review: the user may change scope, iterations, examples, counts, terminology, or pedagogy. **Iterate on the outline until the user clearly confirms.** Only a clear go-ahead ("yes", "create it", "confirmed") unlocks step 4. ### 4. On confirmation — create the files Create under `docs/taskN/`: - `_worksheet.md`, `_questions.md`, `_answers.md` following the formats in `CLAUDE.md` (a/b/c iterations + "Takeaway to say out loud"; one-page reference; New Words table; question parts; reasoned answers). - **Verify everything first.** Compile and run every C program and every trace in the scratchpad; check all arithmetic by hand. In sample debugger transcripts use **Linux/WSL-style** addresses (`0x00007fffffff...`, `libc` frames), never the macOS values this machine prints. Do **not** rely on this machine's stack layout for answers — for question snippets that must be portable, use address variables into **arrays** (element layout is guaranteed) so answers match the students' Ubuntu exactly. Keep any deliberate design constraint (e.g. "int only") silent — it shapes the examples but is never announced to students. - Create the three viewers by copying the most recent slim viewer of each kind (e.g. from `docs/task14/`) and changing **only**: ``, `<body class>` (`worksheet`/`questions`/`answers`), `.brand` text, the topbar stage chips, and the status-line text. Everything else comes from `docs/assets/viewer.css` and `docs/assets/viewer.js`. **A viewer's `.html` basename must exactly equal its `.md` basename** (the shared JS derives the markdown filename from the page URL). - **Update `docs/tasks.html`**: add one `<li>` to the `.tasklist` of whichever topic group the task belongs to (`#linux`, `#c`, `#memory`, `#debug`, `#tools`, `#python`), in task-number order within that group — ```html <li><span class="num">Task N</span> <a class="title" href="taskN/<base>_worksheet.html"><Title></a> <a class="q" href="taskN/<base>_questions.html">Questions</a> <a class="q" href="taskN/<base>_answers.html">ans</a></li> ``` (For a tool/reference task with no question bank, replace the two `.q` links with `<span class="only">worksheet only</span>` or `<span class="only">reference</span>`. Use `Extra Questions`/`extra ans` for an `_extra_` bank.) - **Update `docs/index.html`**: add the number to that group's path chip (e.g. `tasks 3, 5, 7`) and bump the worksheet count in `.facts`. ### 5. Verify and report - Serve `docs/` (`python3 -m http.server`) and confirm every new page and its markdown return 200; confirm each viewer's derived markdown exists. - Report what was created: the files, the worksheet's iterations, the question counts, and confirmation that programs/answers were verified. ## Guardrails - **Never create files before the user confirms the outline** (step 3). - One new idea per iteration; predict-before-reveal; the New Words Telugu table is always the last worksheet section. - Don't announce design constraints to students; don't introduce staged vocabulary early. - Verify by running, not by assuming; keep transcripts Ubuntu/WSL-accurate. - Match the file/viewer conventions exactly so the shared assets keep working. Examples: ```text Unclosed tag: <p> Unexpected closing tag: </div> ``` ## Phase 7 — Queries Add simple DOM queries: ```text --find-tag p --find-id first --find-class intro ``` ## Phase 8 — Testing and Refactoring Create tests for: - Simple elements - Nested elements - Multiple siblings - Text nodes - Attributes - Empty elements - Malformed HTML - Deeply nested HTML --- # 9. C Implementation The C version should give students practice with: - `struct` - Pointers - Dynamic memory allocation - Strings - Arrays or linked lists - Tree structures - Recursion - File I/O - Command-line arguments - Error handling Do not provide the implementation. The students must design and implement the data structures themselves. --- # 10. Python Implementation The Python version should give students practice with: - Classes - Objects - Lists - Dictionaries - Strings - File handling - Exceptions - Recursion - Command-line arguments - Modular programming Again, do not provide the implementation. --- # 11. OpenCode Requirement OpenCode must be an explicit part of the assignment. Students must NOT simply ask: > "Build the complete HTML parser for me." Instead, require them to use an iterative engineering workflow. For example: ```text Problem ↓ Understand ↓ Plan ↓ Design ↓ Implement ↓ Run ↓ Test ↓ Debug ↓ Refactor ↓ Commit ``` Students should use OpenCode to: - Understand requirements - Discuss design alternatives - Create an implementation plan - Implement individual features - Generate tests - Diagnose errors - Refactor code - Review their implementation Require them to keep a record of important prompts and AI decisions. --- # 12. Entire Requirement Students must use Entire during development. The assignment should explain that the purpose is to preserve development context beyond the final source code. Students should examine what Entire records about: - Development sessions - Intent - Decisions - Changes - AI-assisted development - Reasoning/context around changes Students should be asked to compare: **Git alone** versus **Git + development context captured by Entire** The assignment should not prescribe exactly what Entire must capture; students should discover this through actual use. --- # 13. Git Requirements Each implementation must use Git. Require at least **5 meaningful commits**. Do not accept meaningless commits such as: ```text update changes final done ``` Examples of meaningful commits: ```text Create DOM node representation Implement basic HTML parser Add recursive tree printer Add attribute parsing Add malformed HTML detection Add DOM query support ``` Students should be able to explain what changed in each important commit. --- # 14. Two Implementations Students must create: ```text dom-parser-c/ dom-parser-python/ ``` Both implementations must support the same input and produce equivalent DOM tree output. The goal is NOT to copy the C implementation into Python. Students should make appropriate language-specific design decisions. --- # 15. Sample Input Files Create several sample HTML files for the assignment. ### simple.html ```html <html> <body> <h1>Hello</h1> </body> </html> ``` ### nested.html ```html <div> <section> <h1>Title</h1> <p>Hello</p> </section> </div> ``` ### attributes.html ```html <div id="main" class="container"> <p class="intro">Hello</p> <p>World</p> </div> ``` ### siblings.html ```html <ul> <li>One</li> <li>Two</li> <li>Three</li> </ul> ``` ### malformed.html Provide examples containing: - Missing closing tags - Unexpected closing tags - Incorrect nesting --- # 16. Expected Output For each sample input, provide expected tree-style output. Make the examples sufficiently clear that students can test their programs against them. --- # 17. Testing Require students to create automated tests where appropriate. Tests should cover: - Parsing - DOM construction - Tree traversal - Attributes - Text nodes - Error detection - Queries Also require students to perform manual CLI testing. --- # 18. Final Comparison Students must compare the two implementations. Require them to answer questions such as: 1. Which implementation was easier to develop? 2. Why? 3. How did memory management affect the C implementation? 4. What did Python make easier? 5. What was difficult for the AI agent? 6. Where did the AI generate incorrect or poor code? 7. How did they verify AI-generated code? 8. What design decisions did they make themselves? 9. How did OpenCode change their development workflow? 10. What did Entire preserve that Git alone did not? 11. What would another developer need to understand the project six months later? 12. Is source code alone a complete record of software development when AI agents are involved? --- # 19. Final Deliverables Each student must submit: ```text project/ ├── c/ ├── python/ ├── tests/ ├── samples/ ├── README.md └── development-notes/ ``` The exact structure may be adjusted by the student. The repository must contain: - C implementation - Python implementation - Sample HTML files - Tests - README - Git history - OpenCode development evidence - Entire development context - Final comparison/reflection --- # 20. Evaluation Rubric Create a clear rubric totaling 100 marks. Include categories such as: - DOM design — 15 - HTML parsing — 15 - Tree construction — 15 - Tree-style output — 10 - Attributes and queries — 10 - Error handling — 10 - Testing — 10 - C implementation quality — 5 - Python implementation quality — 5 - OpenCode usage — 3 - Entire usage — 2 Adjust the distribution if necessary, but make **actual engineering quality** more important than simply completing features. --- # 21. Important Rules Include these rules prominently: 1. Do not use an existing HTML/DOM parser library. 2. Do not copy an implementation from the Internet. 3. AI-generated code must be understood and verified. 4. Students must be able to explain their own implementation. 5. OpenCode is a development assistant, not a substitute for understanding. 6. Git commits must reflect actual development. 7. Entire must be used throughout development, not added at the end. 8. C and Python implementations must be independently developed. --- # 22. Final Reflection End the assignment with a reflection section titled: **What Does Software Engineering Look Like When AI Writes Code?** Ask students to write a short reflection addressing: > If an AI coding agent can generate a large portion of the source code, what becomes more important for a software engineer? Include prompts around: - Problem understanding - System design - Decomposition - Asking good questions - Verification - Testing - Debugging - Reviewing AI output - Making engineering decisions - Preserving development context --- ## Output expected from you Create the complete assignment as a polished, student-ready document. Do not implement the parser. Do not provide the solution. Do not provide C or Python source code. The final document should contain enough information for a student to start the assignment independently while still leaving the important design and implementation decisions to the student.

entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

entries.name: WebSearch
entries.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

# OpenCode Quick Start Guide

## Linux Installation
The recommended approach is using the install script:
```bash
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
```

Alternatively, install via Homebrew: `brew install anomalyco/tap/opencode`

## Starting in a Project
Navigate to your project directory and launch OpenCode:
```bash
cd /path/to/project
opencode
```

## Connecting a Model Provider
Run the `/connect` command within OpenCode's interface. The documentation recommends trying "OpenCode Zen" for curated, tested models if you're new to LLM providers. You'll need to obtain an API key from your chosen provider and paste it when prompted.

## Project Initialization
Execute `/init` to have OpenCode analyze your project structure and generate an `AGENTS.md` file in the root directory. This file should be committed to Git, as it helps OpenCode understand "the project structure and the coding patterns used."

## Plan vs. Build Modes
OpenCode offers two operational modes toggled via the **Tab** key:

- **Plan Mode**: Disables direct code modifications; instead, it "suggest[s] _how_ it'll implement the feature"
- **Build Mode**: Enables OpenCode to make actual code changes

Start in Plan mode to review the proposed approach before switching to Build mode to execute changes.

# Entire CLI: Key Questions Answered

## Installation & Setup
The documentation states "Install the CLI, connect your agent, and capture the context behind your work," but the provided content doesn't include exact installation commands. You'll need to visit the `/installation` page for specific steps.

Entire works with "Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity CLI, and more." OpenCode is **not mentioned** in the supported agents list.

## What Gets Captured
The system stores:
- **Sessions & Checkpoints**: "Every commit an agent makes becomes a checkpoint: the code change paired with the prompt, reasoning, and tool calls behind it."
- **Context**: Prompts, reasoning, and tool calls are preserved
- **Security**: "Secrets are redacted before anything leaves your machine"

The documentation doesn't specify the exact Git branch naming convention for storage.

The page references commands like "recap and review" for examining agent work, but exact command syntax isn't provided in this excerpt. Check the `/cli-reference` for specific commands.

## Web Dashboard
Yes, there's a web platform: "Capture locally with the CLI. Explore and share history in entire.io." The documentation mentions browsing sessions and reviewing checkpoints on the entire.io platform, though GitHub linkage specifics aren't detailed in this content.

**For exact commands and implementation details, consult the full documentation index** at the URL provided.

# Entire

- [Introduction](https://docs.entire.io/index.md): Coding agents need ideas, decisions, and speed. Entire stores all your code, together with sessions, prompts, and tool calls. And, for maximum agent throughput, it mirrors your Git repos around the world.
- [Quickstart](https://docs.entire.io/quickstart.md): Set up Entire, create your first checkpoint, mirror a GitHub repository, and optionally create an Entire repository.
- [Installation](https://docs.entire.io/installation.md): Install, update, verify, and uninstall the Entire CLI.
- [Entire CLI and entire.io](https://docs.entire.io/platforms/cli-and-entire-io.md): Mirror and clone your repos. Capture, inspect, search, and share the agent-work history recorded by Entire.
- [Overview](https://docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/overview.md): Learn how Entire provides distributed Git hosting for teams and agents.
- [Install the Entire GitHub App](https://docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/github-app-access.md): Authorize the Entire GitHub App and choose which repositories Entire can access.
- [Entire Repositories](https://docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/entire-native-repositories.md): Host repositories on Entire's Git network and push and pull from a region close to you.
- [Mirrors](https://docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/mirrors.md): Connect an existing GitHub repository to Entire with an Entire-backed Git remote.
- [Mirror Repositories in entire.io](https://docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/mirrors-in-entire-io.md): Configure GitHub access, choose repositories, and create mirrors from entire.io.
- [Mirror Repositories in the CLI](https://docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/mirrors-in-cli.md): Create GitHub repository mirrors with the Entire CLI and configure Git remotes.
- [Mirror Access and Permissions](https://docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/mirror-access-and-permissions.md): Understand how repository mirror access follows GitHub collaborator permissions.
- [Entire-Native Branches](https://docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/entire-native-branches.md): Push branches that stay on Entire when GitHub is down.
- [Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/troubleshooting.md): Fix common repository mirror setup, access, clone, fetch, and push issues.
- [Overview](https://docs.entire.io/guides/sessions/overview.md): Enable Entire and automatically store your agent sessions in Git on every push.
- [Capture Sessions and Their Checkpoints](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/capture-checkpoints.md): Learn how Entire captures agent sessions and turns them into committed checkpoints.
- [Session Storage](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/checkpoint-storage.md): Where Entire stores your session and the checkpoints that are linked with your commits.
- [Store Checkpoints in Another Repository](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/store-checkpoints-in-another-repo.md): Push checkpoint history to a repository separate from your source code.
- [Keep Checkpoints Local](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/keep-checkpoints-local.md): Capture checkpoint history without pushing it to a remote repository.
- [Sessions in entire.io](https://docs.entire.io/guides/sessions/sessions-in-entire-io.md): Review session timelines, transcripts, tool calls, files, and attribution in entire.io.
- [List Sessions](https://docs.entire.io/guides/sessions/list-sessions.md): Find active and ended sessions from the CLI.
- [Inspect Sessions in CLI](https://docs.entire.io/guides/sessions/inspect-sessions-in-cli.md): Inspect session metadata, transcript output, and token usage from the CLI.
- [Stop Sessions](https://docs.entire.io/guides/sessions/stop-sessions.md): End stale or active sessions from the CLI.
- [Attach Sessions](https://docs.entire.io/guides/sessions/attach-sessions.md): Link an existing agent session to a commit and checkpoint.
- [Resume Sessions](https://docs.entire.io/guides/sessions/resume-sessions.md): Continue previous agent work from a stopped session or branch.
- [Import Past Sessions](https://docs.entire.io/guides/sessions/import-past-agent-history.md): Bring past local agent sessions into Entire as read-only checkpoints.
- [Inspect Checkpoints](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/inspect-checkpoints.md): Choose how to inspect checkpoint context in entire.io or the Entire CLI.
- [Inspect Checkpoints in entire.io](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/inspect-in-entire-io.md): Open checkpoint details, sessions, and file diffs in entire.io.
- [Inspect Checkpoints in CLI](https://docs.entire.io/guides/checkpoints/inspect-in-cli.md): List, explain, and measure checkpoints from a terminal.
- [Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.io/guides/sessions/troubleshooting.md): Resolve missing, stale, or unlinked sessions, and fix checkpoint capture, linking, and sync issues.
- [Overview](https://docs.entire.io/guides/search/overview.md): Query the code across your repositories and the commits, sessions, and agent work that produced it.
- [Search in entire.io](https://docs.entire.io/guides/search/search-in-entire-io.md): Find past agent work and indexed source code from your browser.
- [Search in the CLI](https://docs.entire.io/guides/search/search-in-cli.md): Search past agent work or indexed source code from the Entire CLI.
- [Use Search with Your Coding Agent](https://docs.entire.io/guides/search/search-from-your-agent.md): Ask your coding agent to search past work and indexed source code instead of running the queries yourself.
- [What Is Indexed and When](https://docs.entire.io/guides/search/what-is-indexed.md): Understand what Search can find, when new content appears, and how repository scope affects results.
- [Search Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.io/guides/search/troubleshooting.md): Fix common semantic search and Code Search issues in the CLI, entire.io, and the `search` Skill.
- [Overview](https://docs.entire.io/guides/brain/overview.md): Give your coding agents shared memory of your project, past decisions, and lessons learned.
- [Getting started with Brain](https://docs.entire.io/guides/brain/quickstart.md): Learn what you can do with Brain and find the right command for each task.
- [Overview](https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/overview.md): entire-graph, a plugin for the Entire CLI that helps your agents find their answers fast and saves token spend by up to 71%.
- [Install and Enable entire-graph](https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/set-up-graph.md): Install entire-graph on your machine, add its instructions to a repository, and verify your coding agent can use it.
- [Use entire-graph with Your Coding Agent](https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/use-graph.md): Ask your coding agent to use entire-graph to find code, trace relationships, and understand what a change could affect.
- [How entire-graph Works](https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/how-graph-works.md): Understand how entire-graph analyzes a repository, guides your coding agent, and works with Search.
- [entire-graph Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/troubleshooting.md): Fix entire-graph install, activation, adoption, cache, and coverage problems.
- [Agent Integrations](https://docs.entire.io/agents/overview.md): Compare Entire's built-in AI coding agent integrations and their capabilities
- [Set Up an Agent](https://docs.entire.io/agents/setup.md): Install, verify, update, and remove Entire agent hooks
- [Antigravity](https://docs.entire.io/agents/antigravity.md): Capture Antigravity CLI prompts, session transcripts, recorded file changes, and token usage with Entire
- [Claude Code](https://docs.entire.io/agents/claude-code.md): Capture Claude Code transcripts, file changes, tool calls, tokens, and subagent sessions with Entire
- [Codex](https://docs.entire.io/agents/codex.md): Capture Codex transcripts, file changes, tokens, and subagent sessions with Entire
- [Copilot CLI](https://docs.entire.io/agents/copilot-cli.md): Capture Copilot CLI transcripts, file changes, tool calls, and token usage with Entire
- [Cursor](https://docs.entire.io/agents/cursor.md): Capture Cursor IDE and CLI transcripts, file changes, tool calls, and subagent sessions with Entire
- [Factory](https://docs.entire.io/agents/factory-droid.md): Capture Factory Droid transcripts, file changes, tool calls, tokens, and subagent sessions with Entire
- [OpenCode](https://docs.entire.io/agents/opencode.md): Capture OpenCode transcripts, file changes, tool calls, and token usage with Entire
- [Pi](https://docs.entire.io/agents/pi.md): Capture Pi transcripts, file changes, tool calls, and token usage with Entire
- [Agent Integration Protocol](https://docs.entire.io/agents/agent-integration-protocol/overview.md): Add support for an AI coding agent that Entire does not ship with
- [Build an Agent Integration](https://docs.entire.io/agents/agent-integration-protocol/build-an-agent-integration.md): Use the external-agents agent skill to add support for another coding agent
- [Architecture](https://docs.entire.io/agents/agent-integration-protocol/architecture.md): How the Entire CLI discovers and communicates with agent integrations
- [Lifecycle](https://docs.entire.io/agents/agent-integration-protocol/lifecycle.md): When the Entire CLI calls each agent integration command
- [Commands](https://docs.entire.io/agents/agent-integration-protocol/commands.md): Required commands and optional capabilities for agent integrations
- [Data Model](https://docs.entire.io/agents/agent-integration-protocol/data-model.md): Data types exchanged between the Entire CLI and agent integrations
- [Dispatches](https://docs.entire.io/guides/dispatches/overview.md): Summarize recent agent work into a shareable markdown update.
- [Dispatches in entire.io](https://docs.entire.io/guides/dispatches/dispatches-in-entire-io.md): Generate and preview Dispatches from the Entire web interface.
- [Dispatches in CLI](https://docs.entire.io/guides/dispatches/dispatches-in-cli.md): Use `entire dispatch` to generate markdown summaries from the terminal.
- [Troubleshooting](https://docs.entire.io/guides/dispatches/troubleshooting.md): Fix common Dispatches visibility, scope, output, and CLI mode issues.

content.text:
Before creating anything, here's the outline for you to review. I checked the tools first: OpenCode is one of the coding agents Entire officially supports (`entire agent add opencode`, or `entire enable --agent opencode`). Entire saves each AI session as a **checkpoint** linked to a git commit, and `entire checkpoint explain ` shows the prompts, transcript and tool calls behind it. The "Git alone vs Git + Entire" comparison can therefore be a concrete exercise for students. ## Task 47: Build a Mini HTML Parser — From HTML to DOM *Subtitle: an AI-Assisted Software Development assignment (OpenCode + Entire + GitHub)* **Base name:** `mini_html_parser`. The main file would be `mini_html_parser_assignment.md`, a new `_assignment` suffix in the same spirit as task 22's `_reference`. It still uses `` and ends with the New Words table. ### Assignment document This is a project brief, not a set of a/b/c observation steps, so it is organised in **phases** instead of iterations. Each phase has four parts: - **Build:** what to build. - **Work with OpenCode:** Plan mode first, then Build mode. - **Done when:** checks against the expected outputs. - **Commit:** the commit that also produces an Entire checkpoint. Each phase ends with a "Say it out loud" line. 1. **Header:** title, subtitle, goal, what's needed, and a "golden rule" blockquote: *"The AI can write the code. You must own the design, the tests, and the reasons."* 2. **Important Rules:** your 8 rules, shown prominently near the top. 3. **Learning objectives** and **problem statement**, with the `html/body/h1/p` example. 4. **The HTML subset:** what is supported and what is out of scope (your list). 5. **Exact output rules,** so outputs can be tested. I'll pin these down: - the tree always starts with a `.` line; - text that is only whitespace is ignored; - other text is trimmed at both ends; - attributes are shown in source order as `[class="intro", id="first"]`; - an empty `

` prints with no children; - several top-level elements are allowed. 6. **DOM data model:** only what each node must hold (element: tag, attributes, children; text: content), with C and Python options mentioned but not chosen for them. 7. **CLI contract,** covering the default tree output and the `--tree`, `--text`, `--find-tag`, `--find-id` and `--find-class` options: - query results print as small trees using the same printer; - errors go to stderr and the program exits with status 1. 8. **Phase 0: setup.** - Install OpenCode and Entire on Ubuntu/WSL. - Create the GitHub repo and run `entire enable --agent opencode`. - Run `/init` to create `AGENTS.md`, then make the first commit. - Look at the first checkpoint. 9. **Phases 1–8,** as in your brief: read, tokenize, build the DOM, tree display, attributes, validation, queries, then testing and refactoring. 10. **The C build and the Python build:** what each is meant to give practice in. Python follows the site's type-hint standard (from task 32), and students run `ruff`/`mypy` (task 34). No solution code anywhere. 11. **OpenCode workflow:** the Problem → … → Commit loop, an example of a bad prompt next to good scoped prompts, and a prompt log to keep in `development-notes/`. 12. **Entire exercise:** pick 3 commits and, for each, compare `git show` with `entire checkpoint explain`, then write down what Entire kept that git didn't. What Entire records is left for them to discover. 13. **Git rules:** at least 5 meaningful commits per language, with good and bad commit message examples. 14. **Samples and expected output:** `simple`, `nested`, `attributes`, `siblings` and an `empty` sample, plus three malformed files (missing close, unexpected close, wrong nesting), each with its exact expected output or error line. 15. **Testing:** golden-file tests, meaning a script that runs **both** programs on every sample and compares each result with its expected file using `diff`. On top of that: unit tests in Python, and a test runner in C. Manual CLI checks are also required. 16. **Deliverables and repo structure,** the **final comparison** (your 12 questions), the **rubric** (out of 100), and the **reflection** "What Does Software Engineering Look Like When AI Writes Code?" 17. **New Words (కొత్త పదాలు):** parser, token, node, DOM, recursion, traversal, golden file, checkpoint, agent, and similar terms. ### Question bank (questions file, then answers) - **A. Multiple choice (about 12):** - DOM tree vs source text, and element vs text node; - why a stack catches bad nesting, and which `├──`/`└──`/`│` symbol goes where; - Plan vs Build mode; - what a checkpoint is, and what makes a commit message meaningful. - **B. Fill in the blanks (about 10).** - **C. Scenarios (about 8):** - draw the tree for a given HTML snippet; - name the first error in a malformed file; - predict what `--find-class` prints; - rewrite poor commit messages; - spot why an AI-written "tree printer" that only re-indents the source breaks the rule; - decide what to check before accepting an AI-written fix. Question titles won't reveal what to observe. The answer key follows the same numbering and explains the reasoning for every answer. ### How I'll check it I'll write a private reference parser in my scratch folder; it won't be shipped and the site won't contain any solution code. I'll use it to produce every expected output and every answer in the bank, so the box-drawing characters and error lines are exactly right. I'll also check each Entire and OpenCode command against their current documentation. ### Decisions I need from you 1. **Repo layout.** Your §14 says two folders, `dom-parser-c/` and `dom-parser-python/`, but §19 says one project with `c/` and `python/`. **I recommend one GitHub repo** with `c/`, `python/`, a shared `samples/` and `expected/`, so both builds are tested against the same files. 2. **Option name.** §7 says `--tags p` but Phase 7 says `--find-tag p`. **I recommend `--find-tag`**, to match `--find-id` and `--find-class`. 3. **Rubric.** Your version gives OpenCode and Entire only 5 out of 100, but getting comfortable with those tools is the goal of this task. I'd use: | Area | Marks | |---|---| | DOM design | 12 | | Parsing | 12 | | Tree construction | 12 | | Tree output | 10 | | Attributes & queries | 8 | | Error handling | 8 | | Testing | 10 | | C quality | 5 | | Python quality | 5 | | Git history | 6 | | OpenCode evidence | 6 | | Entire context | 6 | That keeps engineering at 82 and the process at 18. Or keep yours? 4. **Question bank:** include it, as recommended, or make this assignment-only like tasks 8 and 13? 5. **Topic on the site:** a new **"AI-Assisted Development"** topic (`#aidev`, which also bumps the Topics count to 12), or put it under the existing **AI & LLMs**? 6. **AI model for OpenCode:** what will students connect to? For example OpenCode Zen's free models, or a key you hand out. Phase 0 needs the exact setup step. Change anything above: scope, phases, samples, counts or wording. I'll create the files once you confirm.

### Question bank: mostly tools and process, a little DOM

| Part | Count | DOM | OpenCode / Entire / Git |

| **A. Multiple choice** | 6 | 1: why the tree must come from walking the DOM, not from re-indenting the source | 5: Plan vs Build mode · what `AGENTS.md` is for · what a checkpoint links together · where Entire keeps checkpoints · which prompt is well-scoped |
| **B. Fill in the blanks** | 5 | 1: the stack that catches bad nesting | 4: checkpoint, session, the commit it's attached to, meaningful commit messages |
| **C. Scenarios** | 4 | 1: draw the tree for a snippet and name the first error in a malformed one | 3 (listed below) |
| **D. Reflect on the process** *(new)* | 4 | — | open questions built from your list (below) |

The three process scenarios in Part C:
- A student typed "build the whole parser". What goes wrong, and how would you rewrite it as staged prompts?
- The AI's fix makes one sample pass. What must you check before you commit it?
- A teammate opens commit `a3f…` six months later. What does `git show` tell them, and what does Entire add?

Part D asks:
- What would be lost if only the final code and the git commits survived?
- What did the AI get wrong, and how did you find out?
- Which design decisions were yours, not the AI's?
- Why does working in small steps keep the process visible?

The answer key explains the reasoning for every answer in A–C. Part D has no single right answer, so the key lists **what a strong answer includes** instead.

# Build a Mini HTML Parser — Quiz A quick check of the basics before (and during) the assignment. Try each question first, **then** click **Show answer** to check yourself. Read the reason, not just the letter. --- ## OpenCode **1. OpenCode has a Plan mode and a Build mode. What is the difference?** - A. Plan mode is faster; Build mode is more accurate - B. Plan mode only discusses and proposes; Build mode is allowed to change your files - C. Plan mode writes the tests; Build mode writes the code - D. There is no difference; they are two names for the same mode
Show answer **B.** In Plan mode the agent can read your project and suggest *how* it would do something, but it does not edit your files. Build mode lets it make the changes. Plan first, read the plan, *then* build — that is how you stay in charge of the design.
**2. What is the `AGENTS.md` file that OpenCode can generate for a project?** - A. A list of every person who worked on the project - B. A log of every prompt you have typed - C. A description of the project — its structure and conventions — that the agent reads to understand it - D. A licence file
Show answer **C.** `AGENTS.md` tells the agent what this project is and how its code is organised. It belongs in Git with your code. The agent writes a first version, but **you** should read it and correct anything wrong — a wrong `AGENTS.md` misleads every later session.
**3. Which prompt is the better one to give OpenCode in Phase 5?** - A. `make the parser better` - B. `finish the assignment` - C. `Add attribute parsing: store each name="value" pair on the element in source order, and print them as [name="value", ...]. Don't change the tree printer's branch logic.` - D. `fix everything`
Show answer **C.** It names **one** feature, says exactly what correct looks like, and says what must **not** change. The others give the agent no way to know when it is done — so it guesses, and you get code you did not design.
**4. OpenCode writes a test, and the test passes. What must you still check?**
Show answer That the test's **expected output is actually right**. If the agent misunderstood the rules, it can write wrong code *and* a test that expects the same wrong answer — and it will pass. Work out the expected output by hand (or compare with the sample files in the assignment) before you trust the test.
--- ## Entire **5. In Entire, what is a checkpoint?** - A. A backup copy of your whole hard disk - B. A Git branch for each new feature - C. A code change linked to the agent session behind it — the prompt, the conversation, and the tool calls - D. A test that must pass before you can commit
Show answer **C.** A checkpoint pairs **what changed** (your commit) with **why and how it changed** (the agent session). That pairing is the whole point: Git alone has the first half only.
**6. Where does Entire keep the checkpoint data?** - A. Inside your source files, as comments - B. In your own Git repository, but separate from your source branches - C. In your commit messages - D. Only in the browser, never on your machine
Show answer **B.** Checkpoints live in your own repository, stored apart from your normal branches, so your code history stays clean and the context travels with the repository when you push. You can also browse them on entire.io.
**7. Why must Entire be enabled from the first commit, not at the end?**
Show answer Entire can only record sessions **while they happen**. Turn it on at the end and every earlier decision, wrong attempt, and reason is already gone — you would have checkpoints only for the last few commits, the least interesting ones.
**8. Fill in the blanks:** Git records **______** changed. Entire also records **______** it changed — the prompt and the conversation behind the change.
Show answer Git records **what** changed. Entire also records **why** (and how) it changed. A diff shows the new line; it cannot show the three alternatives you rejected before choosing it.
--- ## Git and GitHub **9. Which of these are meaningful commit messages?** 1. `update` 2. `Add recursive tree printer` 3. `final` 4. `Detect unexpected closing tags` 5. `changes`
Show answer **2 and 4.** Each says what changed, in a few words, in the imperative. `update`, `final`, and `changes` would fit *any* commit in *any* project — so they tell a reader nothing.
**10. Why commit at the end of every phase instead of once at the end?**
Show answer Small commits make the history tell the story of how the program grew, let you go back to the last working state when something breaks, and give Entire a checkpoint per step — so each piece of context sits next to the change it explains.
--- ## The parser **11. Your program prints exactly the right tree for every sample, but it never builds a tree — it just re-indents the HTML text. Does it meet the requirement?**
Show answer **No.** The output must come from **walking a DOM tree in memory**. Re-indenting text can match the samples and still have no tree to query (`--find-class` needs one) and nothing to validate against. Right output from the wrong method still fails.
**12. While parsing, you keep a list of the elements that are open right now. A closing tag arrives. Which open element is the only one it may close?**
Show answer The **innermost** one — the one opened most recently. That is why a **stack** (last in, first out) fits: push on an opening tag, pop on a matching closing tag. In `Bold italic`, `` arrives while `` is innermost — so it is an error: `Unexpected closing tag: (expected )`.
**13. Draw the tree your program must print for this file:** ```html
  1. Read
  2. Write
```
Show answer ```text . └── ol ├── li [class="done"] │ └── "Read" └── li └── "Write" ``` The first `li` has a sibling after it, so it gets `├──` and its child line starts with `│ `. The second `li` is the last child, so it gets `└──` and its child line starts with four spaces. The whitespace between the tags is ignored.

# Build a Mini HTML Parser — Quiz A quick check of the basics before (and during) the assignment. Try each question first, **then** click **Show answer** to check yourself. Read the reason, not just the letter. --- ## OpenCode **1. OpenCode has a Plan mode and a Build mode. What is the difference?** - A. Plan mode is faster; Build mode is more accurate - B. Plan mode only discusses and proposes; Build mode is allowed to change your files - C. Plan mode writes the tests; Build mode writes the code - D. There is no difference; they are two names for the same mode
Show answer **B.** In Plan mode the agent can read your project and suggest *how* it would do something, but it does not edit your files. Build mode lets it make the changes. Plan first, read the plan, *then* build — that is how you stay in charge of the design.
**2. What is the `AGENTS.md` file that OpenCode can generate for a project?** - A. A list of every person who worked on the project - B. A log of every prompt you have typed - C. A description of the project — its structure and conventions — that the agent reads to understand it - D. A licence file
Show answer **C.** `AGENTS.md` tells the agent what this project is and how its code is organised. It belongs in Git with your code. The agent writes a first version, but **you** should read it and correct anything wrong — a wrong `AGENTS.md` misleads every later session.
**3. Which prompt is the better one to give OpenCode in Phase 5?** - A. `make the parser better` - B. `finish the assignment` - C. `Add attribute parsing: store each name="value" pair on the element in source order, and print them as [name="value", ...]. Don't change the tree printer's branch logic.` - D. `fix everything`
Show answer **C.** It names **one** feature, says exactly what correct looks like, and says what must **not** change. The others give the agent no way to know when it is done — so it guesses, and you get code you did not design.
**4. OpenCode writes a test, and the test passes. What must you still check?**
Show answer That the test's **expected output is actually right**. If the agent misunderstood the rules, it can write wrong code *and* a test that expects the same wrong answer — and it will pass. Work out the expected output by hand (or compare with the sample files in the assignment) before you trust the test.
--- ## Entire **5. In Entire, what is a checkpoint?** - A. A backup copy of your whole hard disk - B. A Git branch for each new feature - C. A code change linked to the agent session behind it — the prompt, the conversation, and the tool calls - D. A test that must pass before you can commit
Show answer **C.** A checkpoint pairs **what changed** (your commit) with **why and how it changed** (the agent session). That pairing is the whole point: Git alone has the first half only.
**6. Where does Entire keep the checkpoint data?** - A. Inside your source files, as comments - B. In your own Git repository, but separate from your source branches - C. In your commit messages - D. Only in the browser, never on your machine
Show answer **B.** Checkpoints live in your own repository, stored apart from your normal branches, so your code history stays clean and the context travels with the repository when you push. You can also browse them on entire.io.
**7. Why must Entire be enabled from the first commit, not at the end?**
Show answer Entire can only record sessions **while they happen**. Turn it on at the end and every earlier decision, wrong attempt, and reason is already gone — you would have checkpoints only for the last few commits, the least interesting ones.
**8. Fill in the blanks:** Git records **______** changed. Entire also records **______** it changed — the prompt and the conversation behind the change.
Show answer Git records **what** changed. Entire also records **why** (and how) it changed. A diff shows the new line; it cannot show the three alternatives you rejected before choosing it.
--- ## Git and GitHub **9. Which of these are meaningful commit messages?** 1. `update` 2. `Add recursive tree printer` 3. `final` 4. `Detect unexpected closing tags` 5. `changes`
Show answer **2 and 4.** Each says what changed, in a few words, in the imperative. `update`, `final`, and `changes` would fit *any* commit in *any* project — so they tell a reader nothing.
**10. Why commit at the end of every phase instead of once at the end?**
Show answer Small commits make the history tell the story of how the program grew, let you go back to the last working state when something breaks, and give Entire a checkpoint per step — so each piece of context sits next to the change it explains.

**12. While parsing, you keep a list of the elements that are open right now. A closing tag arrives. Which open element is the only one it may close?**
Show answer The **innermost** one — the one opened most recently. That is why a **stack** (last in, first out) fits: push on an opening tag, pop on a matching closing tag. In `Bold italic`, `` arrives while `` is innermost — so it is an error: `Unexpected closing tag: (expected )`.

+# Build a Mini HTML Parser — Questions
+These questions have **no single right answer**. They are about **your** work: what you did, what you decided, and what you learnt. Write your answers **in your notebook**, in your own words.
+Answer them **as you go**, not only at the end — a question you answer after Phase 3 will get a different (and more honest) answer than one you answer after Phase 8 from memory.
+Before you start, try the **Quiz** for this task to check your basic understanding.
+## Part A — Reflect on the process
+1. Before you wrote any code, what did you think the hardest part of this program would be? After finishing, what actually was?
+2. Pick **one** prompt you gave OpenCode that worked well and **one** that did not. Write both down. What made the difference?
+3. Describe one time the AI generated code that was **wrong** or **poor**. How did you find out — a test, a run, reading the code, or something else?
+4. Name **two** design decisions that were **yours**, not the AI's. Why did you decide that way?
+5. Did splitting the work into phases change what the AI produced? What do you think would have happened if you had asked for the whole parser in one prompt?
+6. Pick one commit. What can you learn about it from Git alone? What more did Entire show you about the same commit?
+7. Was there a moment you **accepted** AI code without fully understanding it? What did you do about it later?
+8. How did you check that a test written by the AI expected the **right** answer?
+9. What did building the parser **twice** — in C, then in Python — teach you that building it once would not have?
+10. Six months from now, another student must continue your project. Apart from the code, what would they need to know? Where would they find it?
+11. Is source code alone a complete record of how software was built when an AI agent helped write it? Why, or why not?

+12. **The big question.** If an AI coding agent can generate a large portion of the source code, what becomes **more** important for a software engineer? Think about: understanding the problem, design, breaking work into steps, asking good questions, verifying, testing, debugging, reviewing AI output, making decisions, and preserving context.
+Answer these in your notebook first. Then turn your answers into the `README.md` of each repository.
+1. **What you built.** What does your program do? How does someone build it, run it, and run its tests?
+2. **How OpenCode was used.** In which phases did you use it, and for what kinds of tasks — understanding, design, code, tests, debugging, review?
+3. **How Entire was used.** What did it record? When did you look at what it recorded, and what did you find there?
+4. **Important prompts and decisions.** Which prompts and which decisions shaped the program the most?
+5. **Bugs you encountered.** List the bugs. For each: how did it show up, how did you find the cause, and how did you fix it?
+6. **C versus Python.** What was different between the two implementations — in design, in effort, in the kinds of bugs?
+7. **What would be lost.** If we kept only the final source code and the Git commits, what information about your work would be gone?
+> Do not complete everything in one step. Work incrementally and keep the development process visible.

+# Build a Mini HTML Parser — Quiz
+A quick check of the basics before (and during) the assignment. Try each question first, **then** click **Show answer** to check yourself. Read the reason, not just the letter.
+**1. OpenCode has a Plan mode and a Build mode. What is the difference?**
+- A. Plan mode is faster; Build mode is more accurate
+- B. Plan mode only discusses and proposes; Build mode is allowed to change your files
+- C. Plan mode writes the tests; Build mode writes the code
+- D. There is no difference; they are two names for the same mode

+**B.** In Plan mode the agent can read your project and suggest *how* it would do something, but it does not edit your files. Build mode lets it make the changes. Plan first, read the plan, *then* build — that is how you stay in charge of the design.
+**2. What is the `AGENTS.md` file that OpenCode can generate for a project?**
+- A. A list of every person who worked on the project
+- B. A log of every prompt you have typed
+- C. A description of the project — its structure and conventions — that the agent reads to understand it

+**C.** `AGENTS.md` tells the agent what this project is and how its code is organised. It belongs in Git with your code. The agent writes a first version, but **you** should read it and correct anything wrong — a wrong `AGENTS.md` misleads every later session.
+**3. Which prompt is the better one to give OpenCode in Phase 5?**
+- C. `Add attribute parsing: store each name="value" pair on the element in source order, and print them as [name="value", ...]. Don't change the tree printer's branch logic.`

+**C.** It names **one** feature, says exactly what correct looks like, and says what must **not** change. The others give the agent no way to know when it is done — so it guesses, and you get code you did not design.
+**4. OpenCode writes a test, and the test passes. What must you still check?**

+That the test's **expected output is actually right**. If the agent misunderstood the rules, it can write wrong code *and* a test that expects the same wrong answer — and it will pass. Work out the expected output by hand (or compare with the sample files in the assignment) before you trust the test.
+**5. In Entire, what is a checkpoint?**
+- A. A backup copy of your whole hard disk
+- B. A Git branch for each new feature
+- C. A code change linked to the agent session behind it — the prompt, the conversation, and the tool calls
+- D. A test that must pass before you can commit
+**C.** A checkpoint pairs **what changed** (your commit) with **why and how it changed** (the agent session). That pairing is the whole point: Git alone has the first half only.
+**6. Where does Entire keep the checkpoint data?**
+- A. Inside your source files, as comments
+- B. In your own Git repository, but separate from your source branches
+- D. Only in the browser, never on your machine

+**B.** Checkpoints live in your own repository, stored apart from your normal branches, so your code history stays clean and the context travels with the repository when you push. You can also browse them on entire.io.
+**7. Why must Entire be enabled from the first commit, not at the end?**

+Entire can only record sessions **while they happen**. Turn it on at the end and every earlier decision, wrong attempt, and reason is already gone — you would have checkpoints only for the last few commits, the least interesting ones.
+**8. Fill in the blanks:** Git records **______** changed. Entire also records **______** it changed — the prompt and the conversation behind the change.
+Git records **what** changed. Entire also records **why** (and how) it changed. A diff shows the new line; it cannot show the three alternatives you rejected before choosing it.
+**9. Which of these are meaningful commit messages?**
+**2 and 4.** Each says what changed, in a few words, in the imperative. `update`, `final`, and `changes` would fit *any* commit in *any* project — so they tell a reader nothing.
+**10. Why commit at the end of every phase instead of once at the end?**

+Small commits make the history tell the story of how the program grew, let you go back to the last working state when something breaks, and give Entire a checkpoint per step — so each piece of context sits next to the change it explains.
+**11. Your program prints exactly the right tree for every sample, but it never builds a tree — it just re-indents the HTML text. Does it meet the requirement?**

+**No.** The output must come from **walking a DOM tree in memory**. Re-indenting text can match the samples and still have no tree to query (`--find-class` needs one) and nothing to validate against. Right output from the wrong method still fails.
+**12. While parsing, you keep a list of the elements that are open right now. A closing tag arrives. Which open element is the only one it may close?**

+The **innermost** one — the one opened most recently. That is why a **stack** (last in, first out) fits: push on an opening tag, pop on a matching closing tag. In `Bold italic`, `` arrives while `` is innermost — so it is an error: `Unexpected closing tag: (expected )`.
+**13. Draw the tree your program must print for this file:**

+The first `li` has a sibling after it, so it gets `├──` and its child line starts with `│   `. The second `li` is the last child, so it gets `└──` and its child line starts with four spaces. The whitespace between the tags is ignored.
